title: Questions in the Temple: Tenants, Taxes, Resurrection, and Love
summary: In the temple courts Jesus tells the parable of the tenants who kill the owner's beloved son, aimed at the leaders who oppose him. He then answers a string of test questions: on paying taxes to Caesar, on the resurrection, and on the greatest commandment. He asks his own question about how the Christ can be David's son and Lord, warns against scribes who defraud widows of their houses, and points his disciples to a poor widow who gives everything she has.
story:
The challenge to Jesus' authority at the end of chapter 11 opens a day of debate in the temple courts. One after another, the groups that held power or influence in Jerusalem come at him: chief priests, scribes, and elders (11:27); Pharisees with the supporters of Herod; Sadducees; and a single scribe. Each tries to trap or test him, and each question reveals more about Jesus and about his questioners. By the end, verse 34 says, no one dared ask him anything more, and Jesus turns the questioning around with a question of his own about the Messiah.

The chapter is the last public teaching of Jesus in Mark. It begins with a parable that tells the story of his coming death to the men who will arrange it, and it ends quietly, with a widow and two small coins. The next chapter begins with Jesus leaving the temple for the last time and predicting that not one stone of it will be left on another (13:1-2), so the chapter's final scene, a poor woman giving her whole living to that temple, is placed with care.
historical:
Several groups appear here, and they did not like each other. The chief priests, scribes, and elders made up the leadership of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish council in Jerusalem, with the high priest (in these years Caiaphas) presiding. The Pharisees were a popular lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and the traditions of the elders. The Herodians were supporters of the Herod family, whose rule in Galilee and Perea depended on Rome; they had first joined the Pharisees against Jesus in Galilee (3:6). The Sadducees were an aristocratic party closely tied to the priesthood. Josephus says they held that souls perish with the body and that they rejected the traditions of the fathers that the Pharisees kept, accepting only what was written (Antiquities 13.297, 18.16-17; Jewish War 2.164-165), and Acts 23:8 adds that they denied angels and spirits. Origen (Against Celsus 1.49) and Hippolytus (Refutation of All Heresies 9.29) later said they accepted only the five books of Moses; scholars debate whether that is accurate or a misunderstanding of their rejection of the oral tradition, but it would explain why Jesus answers them from Exodus. The Sadducees disappear from history after the temple's destruction in AD 70.

The tax question was explosive. When Herod's son Archelaus was deposed in AD 6 and Judea came under direct Roman rule, the legate of Syria, Quirinius, took a census to assess a tribute on the province (Josephus, Antiquities 18.1-10). Judas the Galilean led a revolt against it, teaching that to pay tribute to Rome was to accept mortal masters after God (Jewish War 2.118; compare Acts 5:37), and Josephus traces the later revolutionary movements to his teaching. The tax Mark calls kēnsos (from the Latin census) was that tribute, owed by the people of Judea, where Jesus now stood. Galilee, under Antipas, paid its taxes to him. To say ‘pay’ would anger a crowd that resented Roman rule; to say ‘do not pay’ would be sedition that could be reported to the governor, and Luke says that is exactly the charge later brought to Pilate (Luke 23:2).

The coin Jesus asks for, the denarius, was a silver coin worth about a day's wage for a laborer (Matthew 20:2). The common denarius of Tiberius (emperor AD 14 to 37) carried his laureate head and the legend TI CAESAR DIVI AVG F AVGVSTVS, ‘Tiberius Caesar Augustus, son of the divine Augustus’, and on the reverse a seated female figure with the title PONTIF MAXIM, ‘high priest’. For devout Jews the coin carried both a human image and a claim to divinity. Local bronze coins minted in Judea by the Roman governors avoided the emperor's portrait, which is why Jesus has to ask for a denarius; that his questioners can produce one in the temple courts is part of the point.

The treasury where the widow gives (verses 41 to 44) was in the inner courts. The Mishnah describes thirteen trumpet-shaped chests in the temple, each labeled for a purpose such as new shekels, old shekels, bird offerings, wood, frankincense, and freewill gifts (m. Shekalim 6:1, 6:5). Josephus mentions treasury chambers along the porticoes of the Court of the Women (Jewish War 5.200), and John 8:20 places Jesus' teaching ‘in the treasury’, so the widow's gift was probably made in the court open to all Israelites, women included.
cultural:
Vineyards were a familiar investment. Wealthy owners, often living elsewhere, leased land to tenant farmers for a share of the harvest, and conflict between them was common. The Zenon papyri, the third-century BC archive of an agent of the Egyptian finance minister Apollonius, record the management of Apollonius's vineyard at Beth Anath in Galilee and trouble with the local workers. A new vineyard took several years to bear (Leviticus 19:23-25 forbids eating its fruit for the first three years), so the owner's patience in the parable is long. Jesus' hearers would also hear Isaiah 5:1-7, the Song of the Vineyard, where God plants a vineyard, builds a watchtower and a winepress, and finds only wild grapes; verse 1 echoes that description closely. The Aramaic Targum of Isaiah read the tower as the sanctuary and the winepress as the altar, so the image already pointed at the temple. Some scholars suggest the tenants assumed that land left without an heir could be claimed by those in possession; either way, their hope is as foolish as it is violent.

The Sadducees' question rests on levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5-10): if a man died childless, his brother was to marry the widow, and the first son counted as the dead man's, so that his name and inheritance would continue. The book of Ruth shows a related custom (Ruth 4:5-10). Their story of seven brothers may parody two Jewish stories: Tobit's Sarah, who lost seven husbands (Tobit 3:8), and the seven brothers of 2 Maccabees 7, who died under Antiochus IV confessing that God would raise them to everlasting life.

The Shema, which Jesus quotes in verses 29 and 30, was Israel's central confession, from Deuteronomy 6:4-5. Devout Jews recited it morning and evening (m. Berakhot 1:1-2), the priests in the temple recited it daily with the Ten Commandments (m. Tamid 5:1), and it was written in the tefillin bound on arm and forehead, examples of which have been found at Qumran. The search for the heart of the law was a real question among Jewish teachers: the Talmud tells of Hillel summarizing the Torah for a Gentile with the negative golden rule (b. Shabbat 31a), and Rabbi Akiva called ‘love your neighbor as yourself’ a great principle of the Torah (Sifra on Leviticus 19:18). Later rabbinic tradition counted 613 commandments (b. Makkot 23b).

The scribes' long robes (stolai) marked their learning and status; greetings in the marketplace meant public honor, such as being addressed as rabbi; the chief seats in the synagogue faced the congregation; and places of honor at banquets were the couches nearest the host. How the scribes defrauded widows of their houses is not stated; suggestions include taking fees for legal help, mismanaging estates they held in trust, and exploiting the hospitality of devout women. The law had made widows the special charge of God and Israel (Exodus 22:22-24, Deuteronomy 24:17), and the prophets condemned those who made widows their prey (Isaiah 10:1-2). The widow's two coins were lepta, the smallest bronze coins in circulation in Judea, and Mark explains them in Roman terms: together they made a quadrans, the smallest Roman coin, a quarter of a copper as and a sixty-fourth of a denarius.
literary:
The chapter is a series of controversy dialogues of a kind common in Jewish teaching, in which a question is posed, answered, and the questioner silenced. Mark arranges them with care. A parable of judgment (1 to 12) is followed by three questions put to Jesus, one political (the tax), one theological (the resurrection), and one about the law (the greatest commandment), and then by Jesus' own question (35 to 37), a warning (38 to 40), and an example (41 to 44). The tone shifts as the chapter goes: the first groups come to trap Jesus, the scribe of verse 28 comes in good faith and leaves close to the kingdom, and the day ends with a figure who says nothing at all.

The parable of the tenants is more openly allegorical than most of Jesus' parables. The vineyard is Israel, the owner is God, the servants are the prophets, the beloved son is Jesus, and the tenants are Israel's leaders, who know at once that the parable is about them (verse 12). Its opening sentence borrows the language of Isaiah 5:2 in the Greek; the tenants' words, ‘Come, let us kill him’, match the words of Joseph's brothers in the Greek of Genesis 37:20; and its conclusion quotes Psalm 118:22-23, the same psalm the crowd sang at the entry (11:9-10). In Hebrew the words for son (ben) and stone (even) sound alike, and many scholars think the psalm was chosen partly for that echo.

The chapter is held together by repeated words. The owner sends his ‘beloved son’ (verse 6), the phrase of the voice from heaven at the baptism and the transfiguration (1:11, 9:7). The Sadducees are told they do not know the Scriptures, and Jesus answers them in reverse order, first on the power of God (verse 25), then on the Scriptures (verses 26 and 27). The command to love with ‘all’ (holēs) heart, soul, mind, and strength (verse 30) is answered at the end by the widow who gave ‘all she had to live on’ (holon ton bion, verse 44). The scribes who defraud widows (verse 40) are set directly beside a widow who gives everything (verse 42), and the two stories are meant to be read together.

outline.t: The parable of the wicked tenants

doctrines.note: Jesus presents himself as the beloved son and heir in the parable and as the rejected stone that God makes the cornerstone. With Psalm 110:1 he asks how the Christ can be both David's son and David's Lord: the Messiah is more than a descendant of David restored to a throne; he is the one David's God seats at his right hand, a text the New Testament reads of Christ's exaltation (Acts 2:34-36).

Jesus refuses both revolt and idolatry. The coin bearing Caesar's image may be paid back to Caesar, since rulers have a real, limited claim; but the things of God belong to God, and human beings, made in God's image (Genesis 1:27), owe him themselves. Caesar's claim ends where he claims what is God's.

Against the Sadducees Jesus affirms the resurrection of the dead. God called himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob long after their deaths, and he is not the God of the dead but of the living. The resurrection life will not simply repeat this life's arrangements; it is a new mode of life by the power of God.

Asked for the first commandment, Jesus gives the Shema, the confession that the Lord is one, and the command to love him with the whole self, then joins to it Leviticus 19:18, love of neighbor. No commandment is greater than these two together. Love for God is the root and love for neighbor its necessary fruit.

Jesus condemns scribes who defraud widows of their houses while making long prayers, and he points to a poor widow whose gift the rich overlook. God sees the poor, measures gifts by their cost, and judges religious leaders who exploit the vulnerable more severely (verse 40).

words.note: Geōrgos, farmer, tenant farmer, from the words for earth and work. It occurs nineteen times in the New Testament, most in the three versions of this parable, and five times in this chapter, its only appearances in Mark. The tenants are not owners but stewards who hold the land for another, which is the parable's point: Israel's leaders held God's vineyard in trust, and they treated it as their own.

Agapētos, beloved, often with the sense of only or uniquely dear. It occurs about sixty times in the New Testament and three times in Mark, each of Jesus: the Father's voice at the baptism (1:11), at the transfiguration (9:7), and here (verse 6). The Greek Old Testament uses it for Isaac, Abraham's only son (Genesis 22:2). Its appearance in the parable makes the identification unmistakable: the one beloved son sent last of all is Jesus himself.

Eikōn, image, likeness. It occurs twenty-three times in the New Testament, once in Mark (verse 16). It is the word of the Greek Old Testament in Genesis 1:26-27, where God makes humanity ‘according to the image’ of God. Jesus' question about whose image is on the coin invites hearers to ask whose image they bear. Paul later calls Christ the image of God (2 Corinthians 4:4, Colossians 1:15) and speaks of believers being conformed to his image (Romans 8:29).

Anastasis, resurrection, literally a standing up again. It occurs forty-two times in the New Testament and twice in Mark, both in this debate (verses 18 and 23). It refers to the dead being raised bodily at the end of the age, a hope expressed in Daniel 12:2 and 2 Maccabees 7 and held by the Pharisees. Jesus defends it here, and his own resurrection, predicted three times, will soon give it a first fulfillment.

Agapaō, to love. It occurs about 143 times in the New Testament and five times in Mark: Jesus' love for the rich man (10:21) and four times in this passage (verses 30, 31, and 33). In the Greek Old Testament it translates the Hebrew verb of both Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18 (ahav). The love commanded is not a feeling alone but whole-person devotion and action. Jesus joins two commands that stand far apart in the Torah and makes them one summary of it.

Kurios, lord, master, and in the Greek Old Testament the ordinary rendering of the divine name YHWH. It occurs more than seven hundred times in the New Testament. In verses 29 and 30 it translates the divine name of the Shema; in verse 36 it stands twice in Psalm 110:1, once for YHWH and once for the Hebrew adoni, ‘my lord’. Jesus' question turns on the second: David's Lord cannot simply be David's son.

Chēra, widow. It occurs about twenty-six times in the New Testament and three times in Mark, all in this chapter (verses 40, 42, and 43). In the law and the prophets the widow, with the orphan and the stranger, is the test case of justice (Deuteronomy 10:18, 24:17). The chapter sets the scribes who defraud widows beside a widow who gives all she has.

Bios, life in the sense of livelihood, the means of living, as distinct from zōē, life itself. It occurs ten times in the New Testament, once in Mark (verse 44). The widow put in holon ton bion autēs, ‘her whole living’, which can also be heard as ‘her whole life’. The phrase echoes the command to love God with the whole (holēs) heart in verse 30.

christ:
This chapter shows Jesus as the Son sent after the prophets, the rejected stone who becomes the cornerstone, and the Lord whom David himself addressed. The parable tells the story of Israel's history with God and brings it to its climax. The owner has done everything for the vineyard; he sends servant after servant, and they are beaten, shamed, and killed, as the prophets had been (Jeremiah 7:25-26, 2 Chronicles 24:19-22, Nehemiah 9:26). Last of all he sends ‘one beloved son’ (verse 6). The parable distinguishes the son from all the servants: they are sent as messengers, he is the heir, and his coming is the owner's final appeal. Jesus thus tells the men who will arrange his death that he is not one more prophet but the Son, and that they will kill him. The tenants' words echo Joseph's brothers, and the reader of Genesis knows that God turned that rejection into salvation (Genesis 50:20).

Psalm 118:22-23 adds what the parable could not: the son killed and thrown out of the vineyard is the stone the builders rejected, and God makes him the cornerstone. The early church used the same verse to proclaim the resurrection (Acts 4:10-11, 1 Peter 2:4-7). The parable ends with the vineyard given to others (verse 9), not destroyed; God's purpose for his people continues under new keepers, gathered around the rejected and vindicated Son.

In the debates Jesus shows himself the true interpreter of the Scriptures and the power of God. He gives to Caesar and to God what belongs to each, and he himself, the true image of God, will give himself wholly to God. He answers the Sadducees from the covenant name of God at the burning bush, and his own resurrection, three days after this debate, will be the first fruits of the life he defends. He sums up the law in love for God and neighbor, and in the passion that follows he will fulfill both, loving the Father to the point of the cup in Gethsemane and loving his neighbors to the point of giving his life for many.

Psalm 110:1, which Jesus quotes in verse 36, became the Old Testament text the New Testament cites or alludes to more often than any other, because it speaks of one seated at God's right hand until his enemies are subdued (Acts 2:34-36, 1 Corinthians 15:25, Hebrews 1:13). Jesus leaves his question unanswered here, but he answers it himself at his trial: the high priest will ask whether he is the Christ, the Son of the Blessed, and Jesus will reply that they will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power (14:61-62). He is David's son by descent and David's Lord by right. Finally, the widow who gives her whole living is a small picture of the one who watched her: within days he will give his whole life.
interpretation:
The parable of the tenants was read by the church fathers as a summary of salvation history. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 4.36.1-2) set out the allegory in full: God planted the vineyard in forming humanity and choosing the patriarchs, let it out under the law of Moses, built the tower in choosing Jerusalem, sent the prophets, and at last his Son, and then gave the vineyard to the church. That reading, repeated for centuries, often slid into the claim that God had rejected the Jewish people, a step the text does not take, since Mark says the leaders knew the parable was ‘against them’ and feared the crowd (verse 12). Modern critical scholarship argued first about whether Jesus told allegories at all: Adolf Jülicher, in his great study of the parables at the end of the nineteenth century, held that genuine parables make a single point, and C. H. Dodd (The Parables of the Kingdom, 1935) and Joachim Jeremias tried to recover a simpler original of this one. The discovery of the Gospel of Thomas at Nag Hammadi in 1945, whose saying 65 gives a shorter version followed by the rejected stone (saying 66), sharpened the debate. Klyne Snodgrass (The Parable of the Wicked Tenants, 1983) argued that the parable, with its allegorical features, goes back to Jesus.

The tax saying has had a large political history. Justin Martyr (First Apology 17) cited it to show the emperor that Christians paid their taxes faithfully while worshiping God alone. Tertullian (On Idolatry 15) drew the image argument that many preachers still use: give Caesar the coin that bears his image and give God yourself, since you bear God's. Medieval popes and emperors, Luther's teaching on the two kingdoms (Temporal Authority, 1523), and modern debates on church and state all appealed to it. Titian's The Tribute Money (1516, now in Dresden), painted for the coin cabinet of Alfonso d'Este, is among the earliest paintings of the scene.

The resurrection debate was important to both synagogue and church. The Mishnah excludes from the world to come anyone who says the resurrection of the dead is not taught in the Torah (m. Sanhedrin 10:1), and the Babylonian Talmud gathers rabbinic proofs of resurrection from the Torah (b. Sanhedrin 90b-92a). The second blessing of the Amidah, prayed daily in the synagogue, praises God who gives life to the dead.

The double commandment became a center of Christian ethics. The Didache (1:2) opens its way of life with love of God and of neighbor. Augustine (On Christian Doctrine 1.36.40) taught that anyone who thinks he understands the Scriptures but does not build up this double love has not yet understood them. Søren Kierkegaard's Works of Love (1847) is an extended meditation on ‘you shall love your neighbor as yourself’. Jewish and Christian readers alike have noted that this passage is the Gospels' warmest portrait of a scribe, a scene of agreement between Jesus and a fellow teacher of the law.

Psalm 110 has a double reception. The New Testament reads it of Christ; Justin Martyr reports Jewish teachers of his day applying it to Hezekiah (Dialogue with Trypho 33, 83); the Babylonian Talmud (Nedarim 32b) and Rashi read the psalm of Abraham; and David Hay (Glory at the Right Hand, 1973) traced its many uses in early Christianity.

The widow's offering was read almost universally as praise of sacrificial giving until Addison Wright (Catholic Biblical Quarterly, 1982) argued that Jesus laments a system that drained her; Elizabeth Struthers Malbon (Catholic Biblical Quarterly, 1991) answered by reading the scene in its several contexts in Mark. In the Revised Common Lectionary, Year B, verses 28 to 34 are read on Proper 26 and verses 38 to 44 on Proper 27.
text:
English Bibles differ at several points in this chapter, and a few are visible side by side. Portions of the chapter survive in the third-century papyrus P45.

Verse 4: the King James Version says the tenants cast stones at the second servant, from the Textus Receptus (lithobolēsantes); the earliest manuscripts lack the words. Verse 23: the words ‘when they rise’ are printed in NA28, the SBL edition, and the Textus Receptus but omitted by Westcott and Hort and some other editions, following Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus; the phrase is redundant after ‘in the resurrection’, which could explain either its addition or its loss. Verse 29: the KJV's ‘The first of all the commandments is’ follows later manuscripts. Verse 30: the KJV adds ‘this is the first commandment’, absent from the earliest manuscripts. Verse 33: the KJV adds ‘and with all the soul’ to the scribe's list, bringing it closer to verse 30.

Verse 36: NA28, the SBL edition, and Westcott and Hort read ‘under your feet’ (hupokatō); the Textus Receptus and the Byzantine text read ‘your footstool’ (hupopodion), the wording of the Greek Psalm. English Bibles vary accordingly. The BSB follows the first.

Verse 40: English Bibles differ in wording rather than in text. The Greek katesthiontes means ‘devouring’, which the KJV, ESV, and NIV render ‘devour widows' houses’; the BSB gives the sense as ‘defraud widows of their houses’. The Greek of verses 38 to 40 also changes construction in verse 40, which is why some Bibles begin a new sentence there.

The quotation of Deuteronomy 6:5 in verse 30 has four terms (heart, soul, mind, and strength) where the Hebrew has three (heart, soul, and might). Manuscripts of the Greek Old Testament differ between ‘heart’ and ‘mind’ for the first term, and Mark's list appears to include both. Psalm 110 is Psalm 109 in the Greek and Latin numbering.

teach.big: In the temple Jesus is questioned by every power in Jerusalem and shows himself the beloved Son, the rejected stone, and David's Lord, who claims for God the whole person, affirms the life God gives beyond death, sums up the law in love, and sees the gift of the poor.

outline.t: God's patience with his people runs through prophet after prophet to his beloved Son, and those entrusted with God's vineyard answer to him for what they do with it.
Jesus refuses both revolt and idolatry: give the ruler what is due to him, and give God what bears his image, which is all of you.
Doubts about resurrection come from knowing neither the Scriptures nor the power of God; the God who binds himself to his people by name does not abandon them to death.
The heart of the law is love for the one God with the whole self and love for the neighbor as oneself, and agreeing with that is not yet entering the kingdom.
The Messiah is more than David's son; David calls him Lord, and God seats him at his right hand.
God judges religious display that feeds on the vulnerable more severely, not less.
God measures a gift by what it costs, and he sees the poor whom the powerful overlook.

teach.pitfalls:
The parable of the tenants has been preached as proof that God rejected the Jewish people and replaced them with the church. Mark aims it at the leaders, who knew it was against them, while the crowd protected Jesus (verse 12); the vineyard is given to others, not destroyed, and the first keepers of the new vineyard were Jews. The tax saying is often used to sort life into two neat compartments, a political one owed to the state and a spiritual one owed to God. Jesus' point is that everything belongs to God, including Caesar; the state's claim is real and limited. It is also misused to demand unconditional obedience to government, which the apostles themselves refused when commanded to stop preaching (Acts 5:29).

The Sadducee debate is sometimes used to teach that marriage has no meaning beyond this life, or that the dead become angels. Jesus says the risen will be ‘like the angels’ in not marrying, not that they become angels, and the point is God's power to make new life, not a devaluing of marriage. The great commandment is sometimes preached as ‘love yourself first’; the text assumes self-love and commands love of neighbor. The widow is often turned into an appeal for sacrificial gifts to a church budget, sometimes aimed at those least able to give; read in its setting beside the scribes who defraud widows, the story also warns religious leaders against profiting from the devotion of the poor.
teach.pastoral: The chapter presses on two groups. The first is the grieving, especially widows and widowers, and people who wonder whether they will know those they loved in the resurrection. Jesus' answer to the Sadducees is not that love ends but that God's power makes a life beyond the arrangements of this one, and that the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob keeps hold of those he names. Teach it as comfort, not as a cold denial that relationships matter. The second group is the poor and those who feel their gifts are too small to count. Jesus saw the widow when no one else did. Teachers should be careful never to use her story to pressure people in need to give what they need to live; the same passage condemns those who take the houses of widows.

hard.q: Does Jesus praise the widow for giving everything, or lament a system that took her last coins?
hard.a:
The objection to the traditional reading was put most forcefully by Addison Wright in The Widow's Mites: Praise or Lament? (Catholic Biblical Quarterly, 1982). He noted that the story comes directly after Jesus condemns scribes who defraud widows of their houses (verse 40) and directly before he predicts that the temple will be torn down stone by stone (13:2). Jesus nowhere says the widow did well, and nowhere tells his disciples to imitate her. On this reading Jesus is lamenting that religious teaching had persuaded a destitute woman to give her last means of support to an institution about to fall, and his words ‘all she had to live on’ are a cry of grief. Several later scholars have developed the reading, and it has force for readers who have seen the poor pressed to give to wealthy institutions.

The traditional reading, held by most commentators from the fathers to the present, takes the story as praise. Jesus calls his disciples to him with a solemn ‘Truly I tell you’ (verse 43), a form Mark uses for important teaching, and he measures the gift not by its amount but by its cost: she gave more than all of them. The story fits his teaching that God sees what others overlook, and it anticipates his own self-giving: within days he will give his whole life. Elizabeth Struthers Malbon (Catholic Biblical Quarterly, 1991) read the scene in several contexts in Mark and argued that both the contrast with the scribes and the parallel with Jesus' own coming death matter. Many interpreters now hold both together: Jesus honors her devotion, which is real and costly, while the context indicts a religious system that took advantage of such devotion and a leadership that should have been caring for her. What the story does not do is teach that the poor should give away what they need to live, or that God's favor is bought with money.

hard.q: Does Jesus' argument from Psalm 110 depend on David writing the psalm, and does it deny that the Messiah is David's son?
hard.a:
The objection has several strands. Many modern critical scholars read Psalm 110 as a royal court oracle composed for a king of Judah, spoken by a court prophet or singer about the king (‘my lord’), not by David about a future figure; if so, Jesus' argument that David himself calls the Messiah ‘Lord’ rests on an ascription of authorship scholars no longer accept. Jewish interpreters have long read the psalm otherwise: Justin Martyr reports Jewish teachers of his day applying it to Hezekiah (Dialogue with Trypho 33, 83), and the Babylonian Talmud (Nedarim 32b) and Rashi read it of Abraham. The Masoretic pointing of the second ‘lord’ as adoni, the word for a human superior rather than for God, is often cited against a divine reading. Some critics have also argued that the saying denies the Messiah's Davidic descent, perhaps reflecting a church that could not trace Jesus to David; Rudolf Bultmann considered this a possible origin of the saying.

Responses take several directions. Jesus argues from premises his hearers shared: the psalm's heading ascribes it to David, and first-century Jews generally accepted that, so the question was fair within the debate, whatever modern scholars conclude about the psalm's origin. Evangelical and many Catholic interpreters continue to defend Davidic authorship on the strength of the heading and Jesus' words; others hold that the argument works on the psalm's received meaning among Jesus' hearers, whatever its original setting. The ‘adoni’ objection is answered by noting that Jesus' point does not require the second ‘lord’ to be divine, only superior to David, a son whom his own father must address as lord. As to Davidic descent, the saying does not deny it: Mark has just let Bartimaeus hail Jesus as Son of David without correction (10:47-48), and the crowd at the entry praised David's coming kingdom (11:10). The question ‘how can He be David's son?’ asks how both can be true, and early Christians answered with the resurrection and exaltation (Romans 1:3-4, Acts 2:34-36). Readers are left, as the crowd was, to supply the answer Mark's story gives.

observe: List the groups who question Jesus in this chapter and what each asks. How does each exchange end?
What details in the parable of the tenants (verses 1 to 9) come from Isaiah 5, and what details are new?
What does the scribe add in verse 33 when he repeats Jesus' answer, and how does Jesus respond?
interpret: What does the image on the coin suggest about what belongs to God? Why does Jesus' answer escape the trap without avoiding the question?
How does Jesus' answer to the Sadducees use both the power of God and the Scriptures? Why does he quote God's words at the burning bush?
Why might Mark place the widow's offering immediately after the warning about scribes who defraud widows and just before Jesus predicts the temple's destruction?
apply: If you bear God's image, what would it look like for him to claim all of you, including what you owe to others?
The scribe was not far from the kingdom of God. What is the difference between agreeing with Jesus' teaching and entering the kingdom?
What would it look like for you to give out of poverty rather than surplus, whether of money, time, or attention, and where are you tempted to overlook people God sees?
